goals.title: Kite duels over the island
goals.critique: The sentence is plain, and the loop has real stakes: you build a kite, fly it, duel, and lose it for good, then go back to the bench and build a better one. The road also starts in the right place, with one kite in steady wind to check whether shape alone makes it climb, dive and crash. But kite fighting is an old real-world sport that already has a crowd of games, and in outline this is the paper-plane line from rounds 3 and 4 again (build a flying craft, fly it, learn from the crash). The duel itself rests on string-on-string friction sawing, which is subtle and hard for a player to read, and on a mouse that only pulls and lets out line, which may feel like twitching a slider rather than a skill. The bench, the tears that stay and the patches that change the flight do put worked material and consequence at the centre. Still, the kite never builds or changes the island, and the friends' different flying styles are a sentence each with nothing behind them yet.

goals.title: The sea builds my bridge
goals.critique: This is the sixth version of the sea-builds-land candidate (rounds 3, 4 and 5). It answers last round's three objections head-on: Lumi cannot carry sand, a badly placed stone digs a hole, and a stranded Pickles swims, gets soaked and sulks the next day. The scour is the strongest addition, because a stone can now make things worse, so each placement is a bet and not a paintbrush. The same answer has a cost, though: a rule that sand runs through Lumi's feathers is arbitrary, and it forbids the digging and gathering the human wants. That trades the Minecraft direction for keeping the verb indirect. After six rounds nobody has yet filmed one stone in one surf box and shown a readable tongue of sand or a scour hole forming wave by wave, so the whole pitch still stands on an unproven solver. A sulk is a mild price, and 'the friends roll stones too' is vague.
